context_title:
Build complete software autonomously over hours without human intervention
No stopping, no asking for confirmation, just work
Like me  can work for 200 minutes straight building full applications
This is about the AGENTIC LOOP quality, not about deep research. The key things that make me able to build software for hours:

Plan → Execute → Verify → Fix loop  I plan what to build, execute each step, verify it works, fix errors
Error handling  when something fails, I diagnose and retry
Selfcorrection  I read my own output, test it, fix issues
No artificial limits  I keep going until done
The current implementation has some gaps: the SSE connection times out after 120 seconds which breaks long tasks, the agent doesn't actually test its code after writing it, there's no planning phase before execution, and the iteration limit of 50 is too restrictive. The real solution is switching to a taskbased async architecture with polling so the frontend doesn't timeout, updating the system prompt to explicitly guide the agent through planning, building, testing, and fixing cycles, and removing artificial constraints on how long the agent can work.

I need to add a verify capability so the agent runs code it writes, increase the iteration limit to 200+, and store the agent's state serverside so it persists across reconnections. The backend should handle POST /api/chat by starting a background task and returning a task ID immediately, then stream events through GET /api/task/{id}/events with heartbeats every 15 seconds to keep the connection alive. The task runs in a background thread with full event logging, and the key insight is that the frontend polls a persistent background task rather than relying on a single SSE connection—this way the agent keeps working even if the user refreshes or the connection drops. The system prompt also needs a complete rewrite to emphasize autonomous software building.

entries.answer:
Here is a complete breakdown of everything that was built, how it works, and how to run it.



 What Was Built

A full taskbased async agentic loop — a Python Flask backend + a darkmode web frontend — solving every architectural gap you described.



 Backend: app.py (363 lines)

 The core fix: POST → task ID → SSE polling


POST /api/chat             → Starts background thread, returns {"task_id": "..."} immediately
GET  /api/task/{id}/events → SSE stream with heartbeat every 15s
GET  /api/task/{id}/status → Polling fallback for reconnects
GET  /api/workspace        → Lists all files created by the agent
GET  /api/task/file?path=X → Read any workspace file


The frontend never blocks. The agent thread lives serverside in a global tasks dict — if the browser refreshes or the SSE connection drops, the task keeps running and the frontend reconnects to the same stream. 

 Heartbeat loop (prevents 120s timeout)

python
if now - last_heartbeat >= HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL:  # 15 seconds
    yield f"event: heartbeat\ndata: {json.dumps({'ts': now})}\n\n"
    last_heartbeat = now


This is what kills the original SSE timeout problem. Proxies and CDNs drop idle connections — a 15second heartbeat keeps every hop alive indefinitely.

 Iteration limit: 200

python
MAX_ITERATIONS = 200
while iteration < MAX_ITERATIONS:


Removed the 50iteration ceiling. The agent can now work for ~200 turns, which at typical response times is well over 200 minutes of continuous operation.



 System Prompt: Plan → Build → Test → Fix

The system prompt was completely rewritten to enforce an explicit 4phase cycle. The agent must label every response with its current phase:

[PLAN] — State what's being built, list every file, define success criteria, identify failure points before a single line of code is written.

[BUILD] — Write complete, runnable files. No skeletons, no # rest of code here.

[TEST] — After writing code, always verify it using the bash tool: python3 app.py, import checks, runtime validation.

[FIX] — When tests fail: diagnose the exact error, fix the root cause, retest. Never skip retesting after a fix.

This is the key insight you described — the verify capability comes from explicitly instructing the agent to use its bash tool to run every file it writes.



 Tools Available to the Agent

| Tool | Purpose |
|||
| bash | Run any shell command — Python, pip install, test execution, file ops. 120s max timeout. |
| write_file | Create or overwrite files in /workspace |
| read_file | Read current state of any file for selfcorrection |

All output is sandboxed to /workspace and browsable in the sidebar.



 Frontend: agentic-loop.html (552 lines)

A singlefile web app with:

 Live event feed — each event type (text, tool call, tool result, status, error, done) gets its own styled card with collapsible bodies for tool inputs/outputs
 Phase detection — [PLAN], [BUILD], [TEST], [FIX], [COMPLETE] tags are highlighted inline in the text stream
 Iteration counter in the topbar — updates live as the agent works
 Autoreconnect SSE — if the connection drops, the frontend reconnects with exponential backoff; the backend task is unaffected
 Workspace file browser sidebar — autorefreshes every 10 seconds, colorcoded by extension (.py, .html, .js, .css), click any file to view it
 Stop button — disconnects the frontend (the backend task may continue; you'd need a serverside cancellation flag for hard stop)
 Configurable backend URL — defaults to http://localhost:8000, change it for remote deployments



 How to Run

bash
# 1. Set your API key
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

# 2. Install deps
pip install flask flask-cors anthropic

# 3. Start the backend
python3 app.py
# → http://localhost:8000

# 4. Open the frontend
open frontend/agentic-loop.html


Or with Docker:

bash
docker build -t agentic-loop .
docker run -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY -p 8000:8000 -v $(pwd)/workspace:/workspace agentic-loop




 Files Delivered

 app.py — Flask backend with task registry, SSE streaming, tool execution, workspace API
 frontend/agentic-loop.html — full dark/light mode UI
 requirements.txt — flask, flask-cors, anthropic
 start.sh — onecommand startup script
 Dockerfile — containerized deployment
 README.md — architecture notes
